goals: Choose between statistical, distance and tree-based detectors
Evaluate detectors when labels are rare
why: Fraud, machine failures, cyber intrusions and data-quality errors are rare events. Anomaly detection finds them without needing many labelled examples.
explain: **Statistical**: flag values more than 3 SD from the mean (z-score) or beyond 1.5 × IQR. Simple, and good for single metrics.

**Isolation Forest**: build random trees that split the data at random. Anomalies are few and different, so they get **isolated in very few splits**. A short average path length means a high anomaly score.
**Local Outlier Factor (LOF)**: compares a point's local density with its neighbours' density, which catches points that are odd *for their neighbourhood*.
Evaluation is hard: use the few known incidents to measure **precision at top-k** ("of our 100 highest scores, how many were real?") and involve domain experts in reviewing alerts.

example.title: z-scores and the IQR rule on card spend
steps: New ₹48,000: z ≈ 124. New ₹2,600: z ≈ 3.5, just over the |z| > 3 rule
Both amounts are above the fence
example.result: Both rules flag both amounts, yet ₹2,600 for a festival gift is hardly suspicious. Banks combine the amount with time, merchant and location (for example in an Isolation Forest) instead of blocking on amount alone.

mistakes: Setting "contamination" without any idea of the real anomaly rate.
Ignoring seasonality (a Diwali spike is not an anomaly).
No feedback loop from investigated alerts.
takeaways: Evaluate with precision at top-k and expert review
avoid: When plenty of labelled fraud exists (train a supervised classifier)

practice.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
spend = np.array([1200, 800, 1500, 2000, 950, 1100, 1700, 1300, 900, 1400])
z = (np.array([48000, 2600]) - spend.mean()) / spend.std(ddof=1)
q1, q3 = np.percentile(spend, [25, 75])
print(z.round(1), q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1))                 # [123.9   3.5] 2206.25
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = np.r_[rng.normal(2000, 600, (995, 1)), [[48000], [30000], [25000], [40], [52000]]]
iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.005, random_state=0).fit(X)
print(X[iso.predict(X) == -1].ravel())

check.q: Why are anomalies isolated quickly in an Isolation Forest?
options: They are few and different, so random splits separate them early
check.why: Normal points sit in dense regions needing many splits.

check.q: A good evaluation when only 20 frauds are known?
options: Precision among the top-k scored transactions
check.why: It reflects how useful the alert queue is.

formula.tex: z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}, \qquad \text{flag if } x > Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR} \;\text{ or }\; x < Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR}
formula.plain: The z-score is the distance from the average in standard deviations (flag |z| > 3). The IQR rule flags values beyond the box-plot whiskers, 1.5 interquartile ranges outside the middle half.
